fields.System.Title: INT-3 — Projections
fields.System.Description:
Purpose

Pre-compute the answers that are too slow to work out on demand — and keep them honest.

Scope

In. The availability view, order status view, daily snapshot, rebuild jobs, reconciliation
jobs.

Out. Using a projection to decide anything. Projections are for looking, not for promising.

Design notes

Add a projection only when all three are true: the query is asked often, the honest version
is slow, and slight staleness is acceptable for that specific question. The third condition
kills more candidates than people expect.

Choose sync or async per projection, deliberately. Availability updates in the same
transaction as the movement — it cannot be stale. Order status updates from events — a few
seconds is fine, and keeping it off the dispatch transaction matters more.

INT-304 ships with the projection, not after it. During an incident you need to run the
rebuild, not write it. And testing the rebuild against the incremental update is the only way
to find out that the two disagree — which they will, quietly, every day, until someone checks.

INT-305 is the honesty check. Projections drift, through bugs, missed events, and manual
database changes. The question is only whether you find out. Compare against source on a
schedule and alert on any mismatch.

Every projection row carries last_updated_at, and every response exposes it. A stale
number that admits it is stale is far less dangerous than one that does not.

Risks

| Risk | Reference |
|---|---|
| Projection used for allocation | [doc 09 §12](../../../docs/09-defect-hotspots.md) |
| Projection drifts from source | [doc 08 §10](../../../docs/08-data-sync-and-migrations.md) |
| Rebuild disagrees with incremental update | [doc 08 §5.2](../../../docs/08-data-sync-and-migrations.md) |
| Sync update slowing a hot transaction | [doc 08 §10](../../../docs/08-data-sync-and-migrations.md) |
